docs.D00_original_thesis.md:
Title: The original 2016 food-safety recovery underwriting
Source: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/10/07154952/2016-Annual-Report-Letter-Only.pdf
Date: 2017-03-28

Pershing's 2016 annual letter explains a 9.9% Chipotle stake at an average $405 per share. That is before the June 2024 fifty-for-one split: the comparable split-adjusted cost is $8.10, calculated. This original purchase is distinct from the cost and size of any residual position after subsequent transactions.

The letter's central formulation is: “We have always believed that a good time to buy a great business is when it is in temporary trouble.” Food-safety incidents beginning in late 2015 had damaged sales and reputation. The underwriting was that enhanced protocols plus operational, marketing, technology and governance improvements could restore the business rather than merely engineer a short-lived stock rebound.

The letter says “all of the key drivers of Chipotle’s powerful economic moat and long-term success remain intact.” It identifies a relevant brand, differentiated food and customer value, strong restaurant economics, high returns on capital and throughput. It also cites new restaurants, mobile ordering and catering as opportunities.

A short exact extract describes “Strong unit economics and extremely high returns on capital, driven by a well-honed model that facilitates best-in-class throughput.” This is important because durable unit economics, not just comparable-sales recovery, supported the ability to reinvest at attractive returns.

The product-value argument was explicit: “The product price point offers outstanding value given the quality and quantity of food served.” Affordability and consumer perception were therefore original underwriting pillars, not a response invented for the current slowdown.

The original letter also saw room to strengthen execution and governance. The subsequent appointment of Brian Niccol was not already completed at the initial 2016 purchase; management milestones should not be moved backward in time. The initial investment required a credible improvement path, not a claim that the company already operated flawlessly.

The current review should test brand relevance, transaction frequency, throughput, restaurant returns, reinvestment runway and management execution. Strong realized historical returns would not prove the current growth path is predictable, while weak recent traffic would not by itself prove permanent brand destruction.

No precise initial PSH NAV-at-cost percentage is authenticated in this source extract. The 9.9% figure is ownership of Chipotle, not portfolio weight. Those denominators must remain separate.
docs.D01_business_overview.md:
Title: Company-operated restaurants and the unit-economics flywheel
Source: compiled from: https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-02-04-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FULL-YEAR-2024-RESULTS; https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-10-29-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-THIRD-QUARTER-2025-RESULTS
Date: 2025-10-29

Chipotle sells customizable Mexican-inspired meals, primarily through company-operated restaurants. Unlike a predominantly franchised restaurant system, it recognizes restaurant sales and directly bears food, labor, occupancy and operating costs. Restaurant growth therefore requires real site investment and operating execution rather than only licensing a brand.

At September 30, 2025, it had 3,916 company-owned restaurants, versus 3,726 at year-end 2024 and 3,437 at year-end 2023. More units expand the revenue base, but attractive returns also require new sites to maintain adequate volumes and avoid excessive cannibalization.

The business's prospective moat combines brand, food value, simple menu architecture, customer habit, throughput, supply chain and digital convenience. Chipotlanes improve access for digital orders rather than functioning like traditional order-at-the-speaker drive-throughs. Their value depends on incremental sales and efficient pickup execution.

Q3 digital sales represented 36.7% of food and beverage revenue. That is channel mix, not an independent high-margin software segment. Digital ordering can improve convenience and throughput, but also brings delivery fees, packaging and execution demands. The pack does not assume every digital dollar is incremental.

Q3 total revenue was $3.003 billion, up 7.5%, while comparable sales rose only 0.3%. Average check increased 1.1% and transactions declined 0.8%. New units account for much of the difference between consolidated sales growth and same-restaurant performance.

Restaurant-level operating margin was 24.5% versus 25.5%; consolidated operating margin was 15.9% versus 16.9%. Restaurant-level profit excludes corporate and certain other costs, so it must not be described as shareholders' final operating margin.

Scott Boatwright is CEO. The prior turnaround benefited from Brian Niccol, who departed for Starbucks in 2024. The current company must be evaluated under today's leadership and operating environment rather than assuming identical execution from a past management team.

The restaurant model has substantial growth runway if sites retain attractive returns, but US consumers can substitute other fast-casual chains, conventional fast food, grocery meals or cooking at home. Brand strength and value positioning provide defenses, not immunity from lower visit frequency. The central economic question is whether unit growth, healthy restaurant margins and consistent traffic can coexist as the base expands.
docs.D02_financial_snapshot.md:
Title: Three years of compounding and the 2025 slowdown
Source: compiled from: https://ir.chipotle.com/2023-02-07-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FULL-YEAR-2022-RESULTS; https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-02-04-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FULL-YEAR-2024-RESULTS; https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-10-29-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-THIRD-QUARTER-2025-RESULTS
Date: 2025-10-29

Dollar amounts are millions except EPS. The 2022 EPS figures are divided by 50 to match the June 2024 split; later sources already use adjusted shares. Cash-flow repurchases can differ from management's settlement/excise-tax presentation, so cash-flow definitions are retained.

| Metric | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | 9M2025 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue | 8,634.652 | 9,871.649 | 11,313.853 | 8,942.090 |
| Operating income | 1,160.403 | 1,557.813 | 1,916.333 | 1,515.479 |
| Calculated operating margin | 13.4% | 15.8% | 16.9% | 16.9% |
| Diluted EPS | 0.6408 calculated | 0.89 | 1.11 | 0.89 |
| Operating cash flow | 1,323.179 | 1,783.477 | 2,105.076 | 1,688.082 |
| Property/leasehold capex | 479.164 | 560.731 | 593.603 | 468.881 |
| CFO less capex, calculated | 844.015 | 1,222.746 | 1,511.473 | 1,219.201 |
| Cash-flow repurchases | 830.140 | 592.349 | 1,001.559 | 1,683.720 |
| Restaurants at period-end | 3,187 | 3,437 | 3,726 | 3,916 |

FY2024 restaurant-level margin was 26.7% versus 26.2% in 2023. FY2024 comparable sales rose 7.4%. These strong base-period results make the 2025 traffic slowdown meaningful even though consolidated revenue continues to grow.

Latest Q3 revenue was $3,003.444 million, operating income $477.172 million and diluted EPS $0.29. Diluted weighted-average shares were 1,339.522 million for the quarter and 1,350.159 million for nine months. These are weighted averages, not exact cutoff basic shares.

September cash was $698.743 million, current investments $722.531 million and long-term investments $347.694 million, total $1,768.968 million. No separate conventional funded-debt borrowing line appears in the extracted balance sheet. Large operating-lease liabilities must not be erased by calling the company completely liability-free.

Repurchases exceeded the calculated nine-month CFO-minus-capex residual, implying use of accumulated liquidity as well as current generation. This is not automatically imprudent, but buyback accretion depends on price and sustainable earnings.

A harmonized ROIC series and maintenance-versus-growth capex split are unavailable. Unit economics should not be inferred solely from consolidated margins or an assumed return metric.
docs.D03_latest_results_and_guidance.md:
Title: October 29 — positive sales, negative transactions and another reset
Source: compiled from: https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-10-29-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-THIRD-QUARTER-2025-RESULTS; https://www.cnbc.com/2025/10/30/chipotle-stock-falls-after-q3-earnings-report.html; https://www.reuters.com/business/chipotle-shares-drop-margins-face-heat-tariffs-inflation-2025-10-30
Date: 2025-10-30

Q3 revenue increased 7.5% to $3.003 billion. Comparable restaurant sales rose 0.3%, composed of 1.1% higher average check and 0.8% fewer transactions. Consolidated operating margin declined one percentage point to 15.9%; restaurant-level margin likewise declined one point to 24.5%.

Food, beverage and packaging cost was 30.0% of sales versus 30.6% a year earlier. Improvement in that line did not prevent overall margin pressure. Unit-opening expense, labor, occupancy and other costs must be evaluated separately rather than attributing every profitability movement to food inflation.

Diluted and adjusted diluted EPS were both $0.29 for the quarter. The nine-month diluted EPS was $0.89. Share repurchases can support per-share earnings even when same-restaurant economics slow, so traffic and margins remain important independent tests.

The release forecasts low-single-digit full-year comparable-sales declines and 315–345 restaurant openings in 2025. Its initial February outlook had called for low-to-mid-single-digit comparable-sales growth. Reuters characterizes October as the third sales-forecast reduction of the year.

For 2026, the company plans 350–370 openings, with more than 80% expected to include a Chipotlane. This is an announced expansion plan, not proof of future site-level returns or achieved 2026 growth. The near-term unit pipeline remains robust even as the existing-store sales picture weakens.

Boatwright says “persistent macroeconomic pressures” remain, while pointing to the brand's value proposition. Management priorities include restaurant execution, marketing, menu innovation and more engaging digital experiences. Those actions are identifiable, but the release does not quantify a guaranteed recovery timetable.

CNBC's October 30 report says the CEO described less-frequent visits particularly among customers aged 25–35, and that comparable sales worsened during October. That post-quarter observation matters more for the live run rate than assuming the slightly positive Q3 comp persisted unchanged.

The evidence supports both an intact growth platform and weakening transaction momentum. An analyst should ask whether the problem is temporary household pressure, fixable execution or diminished brand relevance. The company still generates cash and opens restaurants; the forecast range nevertheless depends increasingly on assumptions about traffic recovery and consumer resilience.
docs.D04_price_and_valuation.md:
Title: November 3 valuation after the earnings selloff
Source: compiled from: https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/CMG/history/?period1=1761868800&period2=1762214400; https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-02-04-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FULL-YEAR-2024-RESULTS; https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-10-29-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-THIRD-QUARTER-2025-RESULTS; https://insight.factset.com/sp-500-earnings-season-update-october-31-2025
Date: 2025-11-03

CMG closed November 3 at $31.51 on 33,594,400 shares. It opened at $31.65, traded as high as $32.13 and as low as $31.29. This is an historical unadjusted close, not the current quote shown elsewhere on the retrieved page.

Multiplying that price by Q3 diluted weighted-average shares of 1.339522 billion gives a calculated diluted equity-value proxy of $42.208 billion. Because weighted-average diluted shares differ from cutoff shares outstanding, this is not exact market capitalization.

September cash plus short- and long-term investments totaled $1.769 billion. Subtracting that from the equity proxy gives a simple EV-like value of $40.439 billion before operating leases and other adjustments. It must not be compared blindly with lease-inclusive enterprise values.

FY2024 GAAP EPS was $1.11 and adjusted EPS $1.12. The close therefore represents 28.4x prior-year reported EPS and 28.1x prior-year adjusted EPS. These are backward-looking calculations, not authenticated forward consensus multiples.

FY2024 CFO less property/leasehold spending was $1.511 billion. Against the equity proxy, the calculated historical FCF yield is 3.6%. The nine-month comparable residual is $1.219 billion; no mechanical annualization is supplied because seasonality and new-store spending matter.

Using FY2024 operating income of $1.916 billion gives approximately 21.1x EV-like value to operating income. This is EBIT, not EBITDA. A precise cutoff EV/EBITDA and a normalized EPS estimate have not been authenticated.

FactSet's October 31 public market update reports an S&P 500 forward P/E of 22.9x, compared with five- and ten-year averages of 19.9x and 18.6x. Chipotle's backward-looking ratio is not directly comparable to that forward market metric.

A consistent cutoff 52-week range, historical own-multiple distribution and peer forward valuations remain missing. The original 2016 $405 cost is $8.10 after the fifty-for-one split, but that price is not the cost of the current residual holding.

The current price is materially below recent levels after the earnings reaction. Lower valuation can improve prospective returns only if the earnings trajectory remains sufficiently predictable. The available evidence should not be replaced by a precise-looking forward multiple using an unverified denominator.
docs.D05_market_worries.md:
Title: Consumer frequency, operating leverage and management execution
Source: compiled from: https://www.reuters.com/business/chipotle-shares-drop-margins-face-heat-tariffs-inflation-2025-10-30; https://www.cnbc.com/2025/10/30/chipotle-stock-falls-after-q3-earnings-report.html; https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-10-29-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-THIRD-QUARTER-2025-RESULTS
Date: 2025-10-30

Reuters' Savyata Mishra and Aishwarya Venugopal, October 30, report shares down about 19% after the company's third sales-forecast cut of the year. The account emphasizes tariffs, inflation and tighter US consumer spending. This is an earnings-expectations reset, not evidence of a new food-safety incident.

CNBC's October 30 report highlights less-frequent visits among customers aged 25–35 and worsening October same-store sales. That is a concrete demand mechanism: consumers may still like the product but buy it less often. Brand awareness alone does not protect transaction frequency when household budgets are constrained.

The quarter's 0.3% comparable-sales increase masks a 0.8% transaction decline. Check growth can support revenue while obscuring weaker traffic. If transactions stay weak, a company-operated chain faces operating leverage through labor, occupancy and overhead. Lower throughput can also hurt the experience and economics of a restaurant built around high volume.

Margins offer corroboration: restaurant-level profit fell from 25.5% to 24.5% of sales and consolidated operating margin from 16.9% to 15.9%. Not every expense line worsened; food/packaging cost improved as a percentage of sales. That distinction argues against a simplistic single-cost explanation.

Management execution is another live issue. Niccol's 2024 departure means past turnaround success is not proof that the same operating and marketing judgment persists automatically. Boatwright has an action plan, but its effectiveness should be measured through transactions, throughput, consistency and customer response rather than title or tenure.

The bear case need not assert permanent brand failure. A wider range of plausible traffic outcomes can lower acceptable valuation for a concentrated investor even while the long-run unit opportunity remains substantial. That is different from an allegation that the product has lost all relevance.

The countercase is strong cash generation, thousands of successful restaurants, a robust opening pipeline and continuing consumer value. Menu innovation, better execution and digital engagement could restore frequency. A balanced underwriting must identify what observable evidence would distinguish that recovery from an extended period of weak existing-store growth.

No later quarter, subsequent management statement or future price outcome is included. Current uncertainty should remain uncertainty, not be converted into hindsight.
docs.D06_peer_and_industry_benchmarks.md:
Title: Fast-casual demand is uneven, not uniformly collapsing
Source: compiled from: https://s202.q4cdn.com/514401993/files/doc_financials/2025/q2/CAVA-Group-Q2-2025-Earnings-Release.pdf; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1477815/000162828025038952/q225sweetgreenearningsrele.htm; https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-10-29-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-THIRD-QUARTER-2025-RESULTS
Date: 2025-10-29

CAVA and Sweetgreen are relevant fast-casual comparisons, with important scale, menu, geography and maturity differences. They offer evidence on consumer demand and restaurant economics, not perfect substitutes for a much larger company with a longer operating history.

| Latest included observation | Chipotle Q3 | CAVA Q2 | Sweetgreen Q2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Release date | October 29 | August 12 | August 7 |
| Revenue growth | 7.5% | 20.3% | 0.5% |
| Comparable sales | +0.3% | +2.1% | -7.6% |
| Transactions/traffic | -0.8% | Approximately flat | Not extracted |
| Restaurant-level margin | 24.5% | 26.3% | Not extracted |
| Unit count | 3,916 | 398 | Not extracted |

CAVA's comp increase came primarily from price and product mix, while traffic was approximately flat. It opened 16 net restaurants and its unit count rose 16.7% year over year. The high revenue growth therefore reflects expansion as well as existing-store sales; it is not proof of accelerating traffic.

Sweetgreen reported $185.6 million revenue against $184.6 million, and average unit volume of $2.8 million versus $2.9 million. Its sharp negative comp illustrates that some health-oriented fast-casual demand is under significant pressure. It does not establish that Chipotle will follow the same trajectory.

Restaurant-level margins are non-GAAP measures whose exclusions vary. A 26.3% CAVA ratio cannot automatically be interpreted as superior full-company profitability to Chipotle's 24.5% ratio. Corporate cost, opening expense, maturity and rent accounting need reconciliation.

The broad industry issue is balancing value, frequency and cost inflation. A company can gain share in a weak market while reporting lower traffic, or grow consolidated revenue through openings while unit productivity deteriorates. These distinctions matter for projecting reinvestment returns.

Chipotle's scale, cash generation and established restaurant economics differentiate it from smaller chains. Its size also means new-unit expansion is a smaller percentage of the base than at a young chain, raising the importance of sustained same-store demand.

Exact November 3 forward peer multiples and harmonized FCF yields were not authenticated. No relative-valuation ranking is fabricated. The public operating data provide a concrete benchmark against which to test macro explanations and company-specific execution.
docs.D07_event_timeline.md:
Title: From a long recovery to the 2025 traffic reset
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/10/07154952/2016-Annual-Report-Letter-Only.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/10/07155606/2017-Annual-Report-Letter-Only.pdf; https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-02-04-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FULL-YEAR-2024-RESULTS; https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-10-29-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-THIRD-QUARTER-2025-RESULTS; https://www.cnbc.com/2025/10/30/chipotle-stock-falls-after-q3-earnings-report.html
Date: 2025-11-03

2016: Pershing initiated the position during food-safety-related operating trouble. The subsequent annual letter described a 9.9% company stake at an average $405 pre-split price and a thesis of intact moat plus operational recovery.

2018: Brian Niccol was appointed CEO. Pershing's 2017 annual letter, published in 2018, described him as the right leader to reinvigorate the company. That leadership milestone followed the initial investment rather than preceding it.

June 2024: Chipotle implemented a fifty-for-one split. Historical prices and EPS need consistent conversion. The original average cost becomes $8.10 per current share, but later portfolio transactions change the economics of the remaining position.

2024: Niccol departed for Starbucks and Boatwright took leadership. The company nevertheless finished the year with 7.4% comparable-sales growth, 26.7% restaurant-level margin, more than $2.1 billion CFO and 3,726 restaurants. Those observations establish a strong comparison base.

February 4, 2025: Management initially projected low-to-mid-single-digit full-year comparable-sales growth. The company planned continued restaurant expansion and repurchases after another year of earnings and cash growth.

Through 2025: The growth outlook weakened as consumers visited less frequently. By October, Reuters counted three reductions in the sales forecast. The exact magnitude and dates of every intermediate revision are not reconstructed without primary confirmation.

October 29: Q3 revenue rose 7.5%, but transactions fell 0.8% and restaurant-level margin declined to 24.5%. Full-year comparable-sales guidance became a low-single-digit decline. Management announced 350–370 planned 2026 openings, showing that the unit-development pipeline remained active.

October 30: Public reporting described a roughly 19% earnings-related share-price drop, younger-customer frequency pressure and worsening October comps. This is information about the current run rate, not just the completed quarter.

November 3: Shares closed $31.51 on 33.59 million shares. The review ends here. Later investor transactions and disclosures are not part of the company evidence. The current challenge is deciding whether cash generation and unit expansion outweigh a less predictable traffic and management-execution path.
docs.D08_pershing_context.md:
Title: A residual long-duration holding inside a concentrated portfolio
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/20192925/Pershing-Square-Holdings-Ltd.-June-2025-Interim.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/02210744/Performance-Report-August-2025-PSH.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/15134344/PSH-August-2025-Transparency-Report.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2025/03/14183709/Pershing-Square-Holdings-Ltd.-2024-Annual-Report-1.pdf
Date: 2025-09-15

The August performance report gives gross core-fund AUM of $20.7111 billion, firm assets including Howard Hughes $30.4653 billion, and PSH gross assets $18.5445 billion. These are not identical to PSH net assets or uncommitted cash.

The August transparency report gives PSH NAV of $15.3991 billion, cash 6.55% and debt -20.43% as portfolio weights. The June interim report gives June NAV $14.7146 billion and cash $1.4035 billion. These dated observations establish scale and liquidity without pretending to provide November balances.

The public June portfolio includes Alphabet, Amazon, Brookfield, Chipotle, Fannie/Freddie, Hertz, Hilton, Howard Hughes, Nike exposure, Restaurant Brands, Uber and Universal Music. Exact current weights were not independently reconstructed. A US 13F table would omit some foreign, OTC and derivative positions.

December 2024 PSH owned 21,996,590 Chipotle shares, worth $1.3264 billion or 10.19% of NAV, per the March annual report. That is a historical market allocation, not original cost and not November weight. The position has been monetized in part over its long life; a precise current residual cost basis is unavailable.

The June interim report's discussion preserves the unit-growth and operational case, but ownership itself does not establish the right decision after October's new evidence. A long holding period creates knowledge and a record of successful execution; it can also make anchoring to past performance a risk.

Portfolio fit requires considering restaurant and consumer exposure alongside Hilton, Restaurant Brands and other franchises, while recognizing differences in business models. Company-operated Chipotle has more direct labor/food-cost and site-investment exposure than an asset-light franchisor.

Pershing's stated framework favors predictable cash generation, durable moats, strong management and attractive prospective returns. That framework requires re-underwriting when traffic trends or leadership execution change, even if a long-run restaurant-development runway remains.

No November transaction or later investor explanation is included. The decision should compare current future-return uncertainty with alternative uses of capital, rather than treat original purchase cost or previously realized gains as evidence that the remaining shares must be held.
docs.D09_what_has_changed.md:
Title: Successful recovery is not the same as a stable forward forecast
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/10/07154952/2016-Annual-Report-Letter-Only.pdf; https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-02-04-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-FOURTH-QUARTER-AND-FULL-YEAR-2024-RESULTS; https://ir.chipotle.com/2025-10-29-CHIPOTLE-ANNOUNCES-THIRD-QUARTER-2025-RESULTS; https://www.cnbc.com/2025/10/30/chipotle-stock-falls-after-q3-earnings-report.html
Date: 2025-10-30

The original investment expected a food-safety-related crisis to prove temporary while brand, value, restaurant economics and growth opportunities remained intact. The company subsequently grew to thousands more restaurants than at the original purchase and generated $1.511 billion calculated FCF in 2024. Those are substantial achievements, not evidence to be discarded because the latest quarter disappointed.

Today's problem is different from the original crisis. No new food-safety event is established in these documents. Current evidence concerns visit frequency, consumer budgets, cost leverage and management execution. Reusing the 2016 recovery script without distinguishing the mechanism would be poor underwriting.

The former turnaround leader is no longer CEO. Boatwright has outlined execution, marketing, innovation and digital initiatives, but the next phase requires confidence in that team's results. Past success under Niccol does not guarantee an identical trajectory under different leadership.

Existing-store growth has slowed materially. FY2024 comps rose 7.4%; Q3 2025 comps rose 0.3%, with transactions down 0.8%. October reporting says the current run rate worsened further, and full-year guidance moved from positive low-to-mid-single-digit growth to a low-single-digit decline.

The unit-development opportunity remains. Management expects 315–345 2025 openings and 350–370 in 2026, predominantly with Chipotlanes. A long runway can support value, but only if returns on incremental units and the existing estate remain attractive. New stores cannot indefinitely conceal weak mature-store productivity.

The balance sheet and cash generation are strengths. Nine-month CFO less capex was $1.219 billion, although cash-flow repurchases of $1.684 billion exceeded that residual. Capital allocation therefore also requires a view on sustainable earnings and the price paid.

Valuation has compressed following the earnings reaction. The November 3 close is about 28x FY2024 EPS. That is lower than a higher prior price but does not by itself establish a sufficiently high future IRR. Forward EPS and the traffic-recovery path remain uncertain.

The live distinction is between a great business encountering temporary pressure and a wider outcome distribution that no longer supports concentrated ownership at the current price. The documents supply evidence for both possibilities; they do not resolve the question through later investor actions.

thesis_at_purchase_vs_now: Durable restaurant economics: intact, though challenged by lower throughput [D02, D06]
Brand relevance: intact, but impacted by traffic pressure among key demographics [D04, D06]
Management: broken; original successful turnaround CEO departed and current leadership is in a new, unproven execution phase [D02, D06, D10]
Growth runway: intact, with robust unit expansion plans [D04, D10]
final.valuation_now: Approximately 28x FY2024 EPS; valuation has compressed but remains contingent on an uncertain traffic recovery path [D05, D10]

drivers.driver: The departure of the prior CEO and persistent traffic declines for younger cohorts have impaired our ability to forecast near-term earnings with high certainty [D02, D06, D10]
We are reallocating capital toward opportunities with more predictable return profiles and higher expected IRRs in our current portfolio [D09]

final.memo:
Our investment in the Company was predicated on a successful turnaround and the long-term compounding of a dominant, free-cash-flow-generative business [D00]. While the company remains a high-quality franchise with a significant unit-growth runway, the departure of Brian Niccol introduces a critical period of management transition and execution uncertainty that was not present in our original thesis [D02, D06, D10].

Recent data indicates a material weakening in consumer visit frequency, particularly among the 25–35 demographic, and a negative shift in the company’s same-restaurant sales trajectory [D04, D06]. While the current unit-opening pipeline remains robust, our underwriting requires high confidence in mature-store productivity to ensure attractive returns on incremental site investments [D04, D10]. The current environment, marked by three downward revisions to sales forecasts in 2025, makes it difficult to anchor our forward IRR projections with the degree of certainty we require for a core, concentrated position [D04, D08].

Given the contraction in consolidated operating margins and the potential for operating leverage to exacerbate the impact of declining transaction volume, we believe it is prudent to trim our exposure [D03, D06]. We are not calling for a permanent destruction of the business's moat, but we recognize that the opportunity cost of capital is high [D06, D10]. By trimming, we preserve capital to deploy into higher-conviction, more predictable compounders within our existing library, adhering to our discipline of maintaining a concentrated portfolio that meets our 15-20% return thresholds [D09, D10].

thesis_at_purchase_vs_now: Brand relevance: Intact, but frequency is under pressure [D06, D10]
Unit growth: Intact with 350-370 openings planned for 2026 [D04]
Management execution: New leadership following Brian Niccol's departure; execution path requires validation [D02, D10]
Economic moat: Strong restaurant economics persist, but operating leverage poses risks to profitability when traffic declines [D06, D10]
final.valuation_now: 28.4x FY2024 GAAP EPS, which is lower after the recent selloff but uncertain due to current traffic headwinds [D05, D10]

drivers.driver: Trim position to manage risk and increase capital flexibility given reduced visibility into same-store traffic and leadership transition impacts [D06, D09, D10].

final.memo:
We maintain a long-term belief in Chipotle as a dominant, free-cash-flow-generative business with a durable moat, evidenced by its robust unit-growth pipeline and strong historical performance [D02, D10]. However, the current environment presents a material shift in the predictability of the business [D06, D10]. The departure of Brian Niccol introduces a period of management transition, and the recent slowdown in transaction frequency—particularly among younger consumers—has compromised the near-term comparable-sales trajectory [D02, D04, D06]. 

While the company continues to generate significant cash, the convergence of negative transaction growth and persistent cost pressures has resulted in margin compression, highlighting the risks of operating leverage in a company-operated model [D03, D04, D06]. With 2025 guidance reduced to a comparable-sales decline, the margin of safety at current valuation levels has narrowed relative to our required thresholds for a concentrated position [D04, D05, D10]. 

We have decided to trim our position to prioritize capital flexibility [D09]. This action allows us to maintain exposure to a high-quality franchise while acknowledging the current uncertainty in the traffic-recovery path [D06, D10]. We will continue to monitor restaurant execution and unit-level returns, as our decision to remain invested hinges on the ability of the new management team to restore traffic and justify the business's long-term growth potential [D06, D10].
